nodes.name: Structural causal model (SCM)
nodes.statement: \textbf{Structural causal model}, (SCM)~\citep{pearl1980causality} is a tuple $\mathcal{M} = (G=(\mathbf{V},\mathcal{E}), \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F}, P(.) )$.

nodes.name: Observed variables V
nodes.statement: $\mathbf{V}=\{V_1,..., V_n\}$ is a set of observed variables in the system.

nodes.name: Exogenous variables and unobserved confounders
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{N}$ is a set of independent exogenous random variables where $N_i\in \mathcal{N}$ affects $V_i$ and $\mathcal{U}$ is a set of unobserved confounders each affecting any two observed variables (for $>2$ check Appendix~\ref{sec:non-markov}).

nodes.name: Semi-Markovian causal model
nodes.statement: This refers to the \textbf{semi-Markovian causal model}.

nodes.name: Structural functions, parents and latent confounders
nodes.statement: A set of deterministic functions $\mathcal{F}$=$\{f_{V_1}, f_{V_2},..,f_{V_n}\}$ determines the value of each variable $V_i$ from other observed and unobserved variables as $V_i=f_i(Pa_i, N_i, U_{S_i})$, where $Pa_i\subset \mathbf{V}$ (parents), $N_i \in \mathcal{N}$ (randomness) and $U_{S_i} \subset \mathcal{U}$ (\textbf{latent confounders}) for some $S_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Each observed $V_i$ is set by a deterministic function of its parents $Pa_i$, its noise $N_i$ and latent confounders $U_{S_i}$.

nodes.name: Exogenous distribution and joint distribution
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{P}(.)$ is a product probability distribution over $\mathcal{N}$ and $\mathcal{U}$ and projects a \textbf{joint distribution} $\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{V}}$ over the set of actions $\mathbf{V}$ representing their likelihood.

nodes.name: Acyclic directed mixed graph (ADMG)
nodes.statement: An SCM $\mathcal{M}$, induces an \textbf{acyclic directed mixed graph} (ADMG) $G=(\mathbf{V},\mathcal{E})$ containing nodes for each variable $V_i\in \mathbf{V}$. For each $V_i=f_i(Pa_i, N_i, U_{S_i})$, $Pa_i\subset \mathbf{V}$, we add an edge $V_j \rightarrow V_i\in \mathcal{E}, \forall V_j\in Pa_i$. Thus, $Pa_i(V_i)$ becomes the parent nodes in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: The ADMG induced by an SCM has a node per observed variable and a directed edge from each parent to its child.

nodes.name: Bi-directed edge
nodes.statement: $G$ has a \textbf{bi-directed edge}, $V_i \leftrightarrow V_j \in \mathcal{E}$ between $V_i$ and $V_j$ if and only if they share a latent confounder.

nodes.name: Ancestor
nodes.statement: If a path $V_i \rightarrow \hdots \rightarrow V_j$ exists, then $V_i$ is an ancestor of $V_j$, i.e., $V_i=An(V_j)_{G}$.

nodes.name: Intervention do(x)
nodes.statement: An \textbf{intervention} $\text{do}(x)$ replaces the structural function $f_x$ with $X=x$ and in other structural functions where $X$ occurs.

nodes.name: Post-intervention distribution notation
nodes.statement: The distribution induced on the observed variables $V$ after such an intervention is represented as $\mathcal{P}_{x}({v})$ or $\mathcal{P}({v}|\text{do}(x))$.

nodes.name: Mutilated graph G_{\overline{X}}
nodes.statement: Graphically, it is represented by $G_{\overline{X}}$ where incoming edges to $X$ are removed (marked red).

nodes.name: Notation P(y)
nodes.statement: With a slight abuse of notation, we will use $P(y)$ for both the numerical value $\mathbb{P}(Y=y)$ and the probability distribution $[P(y)]_y$, depending on the context.

nodes.name: Interventional distribution
nodes.statement: Also, $P_x(y)$ refers to the \textbf{interventional distribution} for all $x,y$.

nodes.name: c-component
nodes.statement: Given an ADMG $G$, a maximal subset of nodes where any two nodes are connected by bidirected paths is called a \textbf{c-component} $C(G)$.
differentia: any two nodes are connected by  bidirected paths

nodes.name: c-factor
nodes.statement: For any $S\in C(G)$, $P(S|\text{do}(\mathbf{V}\setminus S))$ is called a c-factor.

nodes.name: Classifier-free diffusion guidance
nodes.statement: \textbf{Classifier-free diffusion guidance~\citep{ho2021classifier}} Let $(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{c})\sim P(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{c})$ be the data distribution and $\mathbf{z}=\{\mathbf{z}_{\lambda}| \lambda \in [\lambda_{min}, \lambda_{max}]\}$ for $\lambda_{min} < \lambda_{max} \in \mathbb{R}$. We corrupt the data as $\mathbf{z}_{\lambda} = \alpha_{\lambda} \mathbf{x} + \sigma_{\lambda} \epsilon$ and optimize the denoising model by taking the gradient step on $\nabla_{\theta} || \epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{\lambda},\mathbf{c})-\epsilon||^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Diffusion training: corrupt data $z_\lambda=\alpha_\lambda x+\sigma_\lambda\epsilon$ and regress the noise with a model conditioned on $c$.

nodes.name: Ancestral sampling
nodes.statement: Given that variables {$\mathbf{V}$} are connected as a directed acyclic graph and we have diffusion models trained to learn the distributions $P(v_i|pa(v_i))$, we can perform \textbf{ancestral sampling} from the joint distribution, $P(\mathbf{v}) = \prod_{V_i\in \mathbf{V}} P(v_i|pa(v_i))$ by making one pass through each model in the topological order while sampling from the conditional distributions~\citep{bishop2006pattern}.
nodes.statement_short: Sample a DAG's joint distribution by drawing each variable from its conditional model in topological order.

nodes.name: Conditional model notation M_V(c)
nodes.statement: We use $M_{V}(c)$ and a square node as notation.

nodes.name: High-dimensional interventional sampling problem
nodes.statement: Given a causal graph $G$, dataset $\mathcal{D}\sim P(\mathbf{v})$, our objective is to generate high-dimensional interventional samples from a query $P(\mathbf{y}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}))$ or a conditional query $P(\mathbf{y}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{z}).$
nodes.statement_short: Given a causal graph and observational data, generate high-dimensional samples from $P(y|do(x))$ or $P(y|do(x),z)$.

nodes.name: Sampling network
nodes.statement: A collection of feedforward models $\{M_{V_i}\}_{\forall_i}$ for a set of variables $\mathbf{V}=\{V_i\}_{\forall_i}$ is said to form a \textbf{sampling network}, $\mathcal{H}$, if the directed graph obtained by connecting each $M_{V_i}$ to $M_{An(V_i)_{G}}$ via incoming edges according to some conditional distribution, is acyclic. Two sampling networks $\mathcal{H}_i, \mathcal{H}_r$ can be merged into a larger network $\mathcal{H}$.

differentia: the directed graph obtained by connecting each $M_{V_i}$ to $M_{An(V_i)_{G}}$ via incoming edges according to some conditional distribution, is acyclic

nodes.section: 3.2 Recursive training of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and interventional sampling
input: causal graph ${\hat{{G}}}$ with ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ having no parents
training data $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{{G}}}]$ sampled from observed distribution $P(\mathbf{V})$

nodes.statement_short: Follows the ID algorithm's seven recursive steps, training conditional generative models at the base cases and merging them into one sampling network. Step 7 applies part of the intervention by generating a new interventional training set.

nodes.name: ConditionalGMs
nodes.statement: \footnotesize \caption{ \footnotesize \texttt{ConditionalGMs}$(\mathbf{Y},$$ \mathbf{X},$$ G, $$ \mathcal{D}, $${{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}},$$ {\hat{{G}}})$ } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \FOR{each $V_i \in \{\mathbf{X} \cup {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}\}$} \addtocounter{ALC@line}{-1} \refstepcounter{ALC@line} \STATE Add node $(V_i, \emptyset)$ to $\mathcal{H}$ \COMMENT{Initialized $\mathcal{H} =\emptyset$} \ENDFOR \FOR{each ${V_i \in \mathbf{Y}}$ in the topological order $\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}$} \STATE Let $M_{V_i}$ be a model trained on $\mathcal{D}[V_i, V_{\pi}^{(i-1)}]$ such that $M_{V_i}(V_{\pi}^{(i-1)})\sim P(v_i|v_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$ \STATE Add node $(V_i, M_{V_i})$ to $\mathcal{H}$ \STATE Add edge $V_j \rightarrow V_i$ to $\mathcal{H}$ for all $V_j \in V_{\pi}^{(i-1)}$ \addtocounter{ALC@line}{-1} \refstepcounter{ALC@line} \ENDFOR \STATE \textbf{Return} $\mathcal{H}$. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.section: 3.2 Recursive training of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and interventional sampling
nodes.statement_short: Train one conditional model per target variable on its topological predecessors and wire them into a sampling network.

nodes.name: MergeNetwork
nodes.statement: \footnotesize \caption{\footnotesize \texttt{MergeNetwork}($\{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{\forall i}$) } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE \textbf{Input:} Set of sampling networks $\{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{\forall i}$. \STATE {\bfseries Output:} A connected DAG sampling network $\mathcal{H}$. \vspace{-3mm} \FOR{ $H_i \in \{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{\forall i}$}\addtocounter{ALC@line}{-1} \refstepcounter{ALC@line} \FOR{$M_{V_j} \in \mathcal{H}_i$} \IF{$M_{V_j} =\emptyset$ and $\exists M_{V_k} \in \mathcal{H}_r, \forall r$ such that $V_j=V_k$ and $M_{V_k} \neq \emptyset$} \STATE $M_{V_j}= M_{V_k}$ \addtocounter{ALC@line}{-1} \refstepcounter{ALC@line} \ENDIF \ENDFOR \ENDFOR \STATE \textbf{Return } $\mathcal{H}= {\{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{\forall i}}$ \COMMENT{All $\mathcal{H}_i$ are connected.} \end{algorithmic}

nodes.statement_short: Connect sampling networks by filling each empty (intervened) node with the model that generates that variable in another network.

nodes.name: Update

nodes.statement_short: Apply the interventions outside $S'$: train ConditionalGMs, sample a do($X_Z$) dataset, and return updated recursion parameters.

nodes.name: Tracking parameters X-hat and G-hat
nodes.statement: Along with the given inputs $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace maintains two extra parameters ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}}$ to keep track of the interventions performed.

nodes.name: Step 1 factorization
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{X}=\emptyset$, we have, $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = P(\mathbf{y})= \sum_{\mathbf{v} \setminus \mathbf{y}} P(\mathbf{v})= \sum_{\mathbf{v} \setminus \mathbf{y}} \prod_{V_i\in \mathbf{V}} P(v_i| v_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$ which is suitable for ancestral sampling.

conclusions: $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = P(\mathbf{y})= \sum_{\mathbf{v} \setminus \mathbf{y}} P(\mathbf{v})= \sum_{\mathbf{v} \setminus \mathbf{y}} \prod_{V_i\in \mathbf{V}} P(v_i| v_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$
nodes.statement_short: With no intervention, $P_x(y)$ is the marginal of the topological factorization, so ancestral sampling applies.

nodes.name: Topological predecessors V_pi^{(i-1)}
nodes.statement: Here, we train each model $M_{V_i}$, $\forall V_i\in \mathbf{V}$ using $V_{\pi}^{(i-1)}$, (i.e., variables that are located earlier in the topological order $\pi$) as inputs to match $P(v_i| v_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$.

nodes.name: Step 6: intervention replaced by conditioning
nodes.statement: This situation allows us to replace the intervention on $\mathbf{X}$ by conditioning on $\mathbf{X}$: $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{{s} \setminus \mathbf{y}} \prod_{V_i\in S} P(v_i| v_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$.

nodes.statement_short: When $G\setminus X$ is one c-component of $G$, $P_x(y)$ is a marginal of the topological conditionals over $S$.

nodes.name: Step 7 equivalence
nodes.statement: Evaluating $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ from $P(\mathbf{v})$ is equivalent to evaluating $P_{\mathbf{x}\cap s'}(\mathbf{y})$ from $P'(\mathbf{v})$ where $P'(\mathbf{v})\coloneqq P_{\mathbf{x}_z}(\mathbf{v})$ is the joint distribution.

conclusions: Evaluating $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ from $P(\mathbf{v})$ is equivalent to evaluating $P_{\mathbf{x}\cap s'}(\mathbf{y})$ from  $P'(\mathbf{v})$
nodes.statement_short: At step 7, $P_x(y)$ equals $P'_{x\cap s'}(y)$ computed from $P'(v)=P_{x_z}(v)$.

nodes.name: Verma constraint
nodes.statement: Note that given access to probability tables, the ID can use any specific value $\mathbf{X}_Z= \mathbf{x}_z$ to calculate $P_{\mathbf{x}_z}(\mathbf{v})$ to get the correct estimation of $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ (Verma constraint~\citep{Verma1990EquivalenceAS, shpitser2008complete}).

nodes.name: Algorithm simulation of ID-GEN for P_{w_1}(y)
nodes.statement: \textbf{Algorithm simulation:} We apply \text{ID-GEN}\xspace to sample from $P_{w_1}(y)$ for the causal graph $G$ in Fig.~\ref{fig:alg-simulation}. Since $G\setminus \{W_1\}$ has three c-components $\{W_2\}, \{X\},\{Y\}$, we first call (i) step 4 of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace. $P_{w_1}(y)$ is factorized as: $\sum_{x,w_2}P_{w_1, x,y }(w_2)$ $P_{w_1, w_2, y}(x) $ $P_{w_1, w_2, x}(y)$. Thus, step 4 will return the sampling networks $\{H_{W_2}, H_{X}, H_{Y}\}$ that can sample from each of these factors. Here, we focus only on $H_{Y}$. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace reaches (ii) step 7 for the query: $P_{w_1, w_2, x}(y)$ since we have $S= G\setminus\{W_1, W_2, X\}=\{Y\}, S'=\{W_1, X,Y\}$ and $S\subset S'$. Here, sampling from $P_{x,w_1,w_2}(y)$ in $G$, with observational training dataset is equivalent to sampling from $P_{x,w_1}(y)$ in ${\hat{{G}}} = G_{\overline{W_2}}$ with $\text{do}(W_2)$ interventional data. With $W_2\sim P(w_2)$, we generate $\mathcal{D}' \sim P_{w_2}(\mathbf{v})$ by calling step 6 (base case). We pass $\mathcal{D}'$ as the dataset parameter for the next recursive call. This step implies that if the recursive call returns a network that is trained on $\mathcal{D}' \sim P_{w_2}(\mathbf{v})$ and can sample from $P_{x,w_1}(y)$ , it can also be used to sample from $P_{w_1, w_2, x}(y)$. Next, since $W_1 \notin An(Y)_G$, at (iii) step 2, we drop $W_1$ from all parameters before the next recursive call. We are at the base case (iv) step 6 with ${\hat{{G}}}: W_2 \rightarrow X \rightarrow Y$. Thus, we train a conditional model $M_Y(W_2, X)$ on $\mathcal{D}'[W_2, X,Y]$ that can sample from $P(y|w_2,x)$. This would be returned as $H_Y$ at step 4 (Fig.~\ref{fig:alg-simulation}:green). Similarly, we can obtain sampling network $H_{W_2}$ and $H_X$ to sample from $P_{w_1, x,y }(w_2)= P(w_2|w_1)$ and $P_{w_1, w_2, y}(x) = \sum_{w_1'} P(x|w_1', w_2) P(w_1')$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:alg-simulation}:blue). We connect these networks and perform ancestral sampling with fixed $w_1$ for $\text{do}(W_1=w_1)$.

nodes.name: Cyclic dependency
nodes.statement: For the graph in Fig.~\ref{fig:cyclic}, $P_{x}(y)$ does not fit any familiar criterion such as backdoor or front door. ID algorithm factorizes $P_{x}(y)$ into c-factors at its step 4, as $ P_{x}(y)= \sum_{w_1,w_2} P_{x,w_1}(w_2) P_{x,w_2}(w_1,y)$ and estimates each of them recursively. Suppose we naively design an algorithm that follow ID step-by-step and trains a generative model and sample from every factor it encounters. This algorithm would not know which of these factors to learn and sample first with the generative models. To sample $W_2 \sim P_{x,w_1}(w_2)$ we need $W_1$ as input, which has to be sampled from $P_{x,w_2}(w_1,y)$. But to sample $\{W_1, Y\} \sim P_{x,w_2}(w_1,y)$, we need $W_2$ as input which has to be sampled from $P_{x,w_1}(w_2)$. Therefore, no order helps to sample all $W_1, W_2,Y$ consistently. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace follows ID's recursive trace to reach at the factorization: $ P_{x}(y)= \sum_{w_1,w_2} P_{x,w_1}(w_2) P_{x,w_2}(w_1,y)$ but solves the deadlock issue by avoiding direct sampling from them. Rather, it first trains the required models for c-components $\{W_1,Y\},\{W_2\}$ individually, considering all possible input values, and then connects them to perform sampling. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace first obtains $P_{x,w_2}(w_1,y) = P(w_1|x)P(y|x,w_1,w_2)$, and trains a conditional model for each of the conditional distributions (Fig.~\ref{fig:cyclic} left-blue). Similarly, for $P_{x, w_1}(w_2) = \sum_{x'}P(x')P(w_2|x', w_1)$, we train models for each conditional distribution (right-blue). Note that $X$ and $X'$ are sampled from the same $P(x)$ but considered as different variables. Thus, we train $M_{X'}$ to sample from $P(x')$ which is different from intervention $\text{do}(X)$. Finally, we merge these networks trained for each c-component to build a single sampling network and can perform ancestral sampling on this network to sample from $P_{x}(y), \forall x$.

For the c-component $\{W_1,Y\}$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace first obtains $P_{x,w_2}(w_1,y) = P(w_1|x)P(y|x,w_1,w_2)$, and trains conditional models $M_{W_1}$ and $M_{Y}$ for these conditional distributions. Similarly, for $\{W_2\}$, we have $P_{x, w_1}(w_2) = \sum_{x'}P(x')P(w_2|x', w_1)$ and we train $M_{X'}$ and $M_{W_2}$. Finally, we merge these networks based on inputs-outputs to build a single sampling network and perform ancestral sampling on it to sample from $P_{x}(y), \forall x$.

nodes.name: Complexity analysis of ID-GEN
nodes.statement: \citet{bhattacharyya2022efficient} in their work discusses the sample complexity and time complexity of \citet{shpitser2008complete}'s ID algorithm. Since our algorithm \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is build upon the recursive structure of ID, we follow their approach to determine the computational complexity of our algorithm. Suppose, in step 4 \text{ID-GEN}\xspace factorizes $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ as $${\textstyle\sum}_{\mathbf{v}\setminus(\mathbf{y}\cup \mathbf{x})} P_{\mathbf{v}\setminus s_1}(s_1) \hdots P_{\mathbf{v}\setminus s_l}(s_l) \hdots P_{\mathbf{v}\setminus s_n}(s_n)$$ where each $S_i$ is the c-factor of each c-component $C_i$. Let the number of variables located in each c-component be $k$. Suppose, the intervention $\mathbf{X}$ can be partitioned into multiple c-components and the c-components can be arranged in a way such that $\mathbf{X}= \cup^{l}_{i=1} \mathbf{X}_i$ and $\mathbf{X}_i \subseteq C_i$, i.e., all interventions are located in the first $l$ c-components. Following~\cite{bhattacharyya2022efficient}, we define two sets $\mathbf{C}_{>l}= \cup_{i>l} C_i$ and $\mathbf{C}_{\leq l}= \cup_{i\leq l} C_i$. For $|\mathbf{C}_{>l}|= n-l$, c-components that do not contain any $\mathbf{X}$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace will either go to step1 or step 6. In the base cases, they will train $k$ models for each c-components. Thus, the number of models trained for these c-components will be $\mathcal{O}((n-l)k)$. For the first $|\mathbf{C}_{\leq l}|= l$, c-components, we assume that each c-component contains intervention subset $\mathbf{X}_i$ of size $\mathcal{X}$. Then the size of the remaining c-component is $k-\mathcal{X}$. For each $P_{\mathbf{v}\setminus s_i}(s_i)$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace will eventually reach the base cases: Step 1 or 6 and will train $k-\mathcal{X}$ models. Now, consider recursive steps. We assume that, in the worst case, $\mathbf{X}_i$ will reduce one at a time, by visiting step 7 and step 2 alternately. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace will visit step 7, $\mathcal{O}((\mathcal{X}/2-1))$ times (except base case). Whenever \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step 7, it will apply a subset of the intervention $\mathbf{X}_i$ and atmost $k$ models will be trained to sample the updated training dataset. Thus, till the base case, the total number of models trained in step 7s will be $\mathcal{O}(k(\mathcal{X}/2-1))$. If we consider the whole recursive route for each c-component $C_i\in \mathbf{C}_{\leq l}$, we will train $\mathcal{O}(k(\mathcal{X}/2-1)) + \mathcal{O}((k-\mathcal{X})) = \mathcal{O}(k\mathcal{X}/2)$ number of models. For all c-components in $\mathbf{C}_{\leq l}$, we will train $\mathcal{O}(lk\mathcal{X}/2)$ number of models. Finally, if we consider all c-components, we will train in total $\mathcal{O}((n-l)k + lk\mathcal{X}/2)$ models. If the cost of training a diffusion model to learn a specific conditional distribution is $\mathcal{O}(T)$, then the total training cost is $\mathcal{O}(T(n-l)k + Tlk\mathcal{X}/2).$ Note that, when there exists no confounders, we have $k=1$ and the trining cost is $\mathcal{O}(T(n-l) + Tl)= \mathcal{O}(Tn)$. Here $|An(\mathbf{Y})_G| = n$. Existing algorithms train $|\mathbf{V}|$ number of models for a causal graph of $\mathbf{V}$ variables. Thus, their training cost is $\mathcal{O}(T|\mathbf{V}|)$.
nodes.statement_short: Counting argument over c-components following Bhattacharyya et al.: base cases train $k$ models per c-component and each step-7 visit at most $k$ more. Total $O((n-l)k+lk\mathcal{X}/2)$ models, $O(Tn)$ without confounders.

nodes.name: Proof of the recursive trace lemma
nodes.statement: Suppose, both algorithms start with an input causal query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ for a given graph $G$. For this query, the parameters $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, G$ of ID$(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}', \mathcal{D}, G)$ represent the same objects: the set of observed variables $\mathbf{Y}$, the set of intervened variables $\mathbf{X}$ and the causal graph $G$. According to Proposition~\ref{prop:step-decide}, Algorithm~\ref{alg:id-dag}: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and Algorithm~\ref{alg:ID}: ID only check these 3 parameters to enter into any steps and decide the next recursive step. Thus, we use proof by induction based on these 3 parameters to prove our statement. \textbf{Induction base case (recursion level $R=0$): } Both algorithms start with the same input causal query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ in $G$, i.e., the same parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, G$. We show that at recursion level $R=0$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step $i$ if and only if ID enters step $i$ for any $i\in [7]$. \textbf{Step 1:} Both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if the intervention set $\mathbf{X}$ is empty and go to step 1. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 1 iff ID enters step 1. \textbf{Step 2:} If the condition for step 1 is not satisfied, then both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if there exist any non-ancestor variables of $\mathbf{Y}$: $\mathbf{V} \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G$ in the graph to enter in their corresponding step 2. Thus, with the same $\mathbf{Y}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 2 iff ID enters step 2. \textbf{Step 3:} If conditions for Steps [1-2] are not satisfied, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if $\mathbf{W}$ is an empty set for $\mathbf{W} = (\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}) \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_{G_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}$ to enter in their corresponding step 3. Since both algorithms have the same $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 3 iff ID enters step 3. \textbf{Step 4:} If conditions for Steps [1-3] are not satisfied, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if they can partition the variables set $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})$ into $k$ (multiple) c-components. Since these condition checks depend on $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$ and both have the same input $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 4 iff ID enters step 4. \textbf{Step 5:} If conditions for Steps [1-4] are not satisfied, both algorithms check if $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and $C(G) = \{G\}$ to enter their corresponding step 5. Since both have the same $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 5 iff ID enters step 5. \textbf{Step 6:} If the conditions of Steps [1-5] are not satisfied, ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and $S \in C(G)$, to enter their corresponding step 6. Since both have the same $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 6 iff ID enters step 6. \textbf{Step 7:} If conditions for Steps [1-6] are not satisfied, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and ($\exists S'$) such that $S \subset S' \in C(G)$ to enter their corresponding step 7. Since both have the same $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, both will satisfy this condition and enter this step. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 7 iff ID enters step 7. \textbf{Induction Hypothesis:} We assume that for recursion levels $R=1,\hdots,r$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID follow the same steps at each recursion level and maintain the same values for the parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}$ and $G$. \textbf{Inductive steps:} Both algorithms have the same set of parameters $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, G$ and they are at the same step $i$ at the current recursion level $R=r$. As inductive step, we show that with the same values of the parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}$ and $G$ at recursion level $R=r$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID will visit the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$. \textbf{Step 1}: Step 1 is a base case of both algorithms. After entering into step 1 with $\mathbf{X}=\emptyset$, ID estimates $\sum_{\mathbf{v}\setminus y}P(\mathbf{v})$ and ends the recursion. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace also ends the recursion after training a set of conditional models $M_{V_i}(V_{\pi}^{(i-1)})\sim P(v_i|v_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace goes to the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$ iff ID goes to the same step which in this case is \texttt{Return}. \textbf{Step 2}: At step 2, both \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID update their intervention set $\mathbf{X}$ as $\mathbf{X}\cap An(\mathbf{Y})_G$ and the causal graph $G$ as $ G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}$. The same values of the parameters $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}$ and $G$ will lead both algorithms to the same step at the recursion level $R=r+1$. Thus, at recursion level $R=r+1$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step $i$ iff ID visits step $i$, $\forall i \in [7]$. \textbf{Step 3}: At step 3, both algorithms only update the intervention set parameter $\mathbf{X}$ as $\mathbf{X}= \mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{W}$ and perform the next recursive call. Since they leave for the next recursive call with the same set of parameters, at recursion level $R=r+1$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step $i$ iff ID visits step $i$, $\forall i \in [7]$. \textbf{Step 4}: At step 4, both \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID partition the variables set $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})$ into $k$ (multiple) c-components. Then they perform a recursive call for each c-component with parameter $\mathbf{Y}=S_i$ and $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V}\setminus S_i$. For each of these $k$ recursive calls, both algorithms use the same values for the parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}$ and $G$. Thus, at recursion level $R=r+1$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step $i$ iff ID visits step $i$, $\forall i \in [7]$. \textbf{Step 5}: Step 5 is a base case for both algorithms, and if both algorithms are at step 5, they return \texttt{FAIL}. This step represents the non-identifiability case. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace goes to the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$ iff ID goes to the same step, which in this case is \texttt{Return}. \textbf{Step 6}: Step 6 is a base case for both algorithms. ID calculates the product of a set of conditional distributions $P(v_i|v^{i-1}_{\pi})$ and returns it. While \text{ID-GEN}\xspace trains conditional models $M_{V_i}(V_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$ to learn those conditional distributions, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns a sampling network after connecting these models. Both algorithms end the recursion here and return different objects but that will not affect their future trace. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace goes to the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$ iff ID goes to the same step which in this case is \texttt{Return}. \textbf{Step 7}: ID algorithm at step 7, updates its distribution parameter $P$ with $P_{\mathbf{x_z}}(S')$. nodes.name: Same parameters, induct on them
nodes.statement: Suppose, both algorithms start with an input causal query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ for a given graph $G$. Thus, we use proof by induction based on these 3 parameters to prove our statement.

nodes.name: Base case R=0
nodes.statement: \textbf{Induction base case (recursion level $R=0$): } Both algorithms start with the same input causal query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ in $G$, i.e., the same parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, G$. We show that at recursion level $R=0$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step $i$ if and only if ID enters step $i$ for any $i\in [7]$. \textbf{Step 1:} Both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if the intervention set $\mathbf{X}$ is empty and go to step 1. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 1 iff ID enters step 1. \textbf{Step 2:} If the condition for step 1 is not satisfied, then both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if there exist any non-ancestor variables of $\mathbf{Y}$: $\mathbf{V} \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G$ in the graph to enter in their corresponding step 2. Thus, with the same $\mathbf{Y}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 2 iff ID enters step 2. \textbf{Step 3:} If conditions for Steps [1-2] are not satisfied, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if $\mathbf{W}$ is an empty set for $\mathbf{W} = (\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}) \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_{G_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}$ to enter in their corresponding step 3. Since both algorithms have the same $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 3 iff ID enters step 3. \textbf{Step 4:} If conditions for Steps [1-3] are not satisfied, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if they can partition the variables set $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})$ into $k$ (multiple) c-components. Since these condition checks depend on $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$ and both have the same input $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 4 iff ID enters step 4. \textbf{Step 5:} If conditions for Steps [1-4] are not satisfied, both algorithms check if $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and $C(G) = \{G\}$ to enter their corresponding step 5. Since both have the same $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 5 iff ID enters step 5. \textbf{Step 6:} If the conditions of Steps [1-5] are not satisfied, ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and $S \in C(G)$, to enter their corresponding step 6. Since both have the same $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 6 iff ID enters step 6. \textbf{Step 7:} If conditions for Steps [1-6] are not satisfied, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace check if $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and ($\exists S'$) such that $S \subset S' \in C(G)$ to enter their corresponding step 7. Since both have the same $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$, both will satisfy this condition and enter this step. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters step 7 iff ID enters step 7.
nodes.statement_short: At level 0 both enter the same step.

nodes.statement: \textbf{Induction Hypothesis:} We assume that for recursion levels $R=1,\hdots,r$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID follow the same steps at each recursion level and maintain the same values for the parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}$ and $G$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inductive steps:} Both algorithms have the same set of parameters $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, G$ and they are at the same step $i$ at the current recursion level $R=r$. As inductive step, we show that with the same values of the parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}$ and $G$ at recursion level $R=r$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID will visit the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$. \textbf{Step 1}: Step 1 is a base case of both algorithms. After entering into step 1 with $\mathbf{X}=\emptyset$, ID estimates $\sum_{\mathbf{v}\setminus y}P(\mathbf{v})$ and ends the recursion. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace also ends the recursion after training a set of conditional models $M_{V_i}(V_{\pi}^{(i-1)})\sim P(v_i|v_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace goes to the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$ iff ID goes to the same step which in this case is \texttt{Return}. \textbf{Step 2}: At step 2, both \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID update their intervention set $\mathbf{X}$ as $\mathbf{X}\cap An(\mathbf{Y})_G$ and the causal graph $G$ as $ G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}$. The same values of the parameters $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}$ and $G$ will lead both algorithms to the same step at the recursion level $R=r+1$. Thus, at recursion level $R=r+1$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step $i$ iff ID visits step $i$, $\forall i \in [7]$. \textbf{Step 3}: At step 3, both algorithms only update the intervention set parameter $\mathbf{X}$ as $\mathbf{X}= \mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{W}$ and perform the next recursive call. Since they leave for the next recursive call with the same set of parameters, at recursion level $R=r+1$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step $i$ iff ID visits step $i$, $\forall i \in [7]$. \textbf{Step 4}: At step 4, both \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID partition the variables set $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})$ into $k$ (multiple) c-components. Then they perform a recursive call for each c-component with parameter $\mathbf{Y}=S_i$ and $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V}\setminus S_i$. For each of these $k$ recursive calls, both algorithms use the same values for the parameter set $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}$ and $G$. Thus, at recursion level $R=r+1$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step $i$ iff ID visits step $i$, $\forall i \in [7]$. \textbf{Step 5}: Step 5 is a base case for both algorithms, and if both algorithms are at step 5, they return \texttt{FAIL}. This step represents the non-identifiability case. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace goes to the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$ iff ID goes to the same step, which in this case is \texttt{Return}. \textbf{Step 6}: Step 6 is a base case for both algorithms. ID calculates the product of a set of conditional distributions $P(v_i|v^{i-1}_{\pi})$ and returns it. While \text{ID-GEN}\xspace trains conditional models $M_{V_i}(V_{\pi}^{(i-1)})$ to learn those conditional distributions, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns a sampling network after connecting these models. Both algorithms end the recursion here and return different objects but that will not affect their future trace. Thus, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace goes to the same step at recursion level $R=r+1$ iff ID goes to the same step which in this case is \texttt{Return}. \textbf{Step 7}: ID algorithm at step 7, updates its distribution parameter $P$ with $P_{\mathbf{x_z}}(S')$. On the other hand, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace generates $\text{do}(\mathbf{X_Z})$ interventional samples. Both algorithms update their parameters set $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}$ and $G$ in the same way as $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}= \mathbf{X} \cap S'$ (or $\mathbf{X}\setminus \mathbf{X}_Z$ since $\mathbf{X} \cap S'= \mathbf{X}\setminus \mathbf{X}_Z$) and $G= G_{S'}$. Since they leave for the next recursive call with the same set of parameters $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, G$, at recursion level $R=r+1$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step $i$ iff ID visits step $i$, $\forall i \in [7]$.

Since ID is complete, the query -- whether it is identifiable or not -- terminates in one of the steps 1, 5, or 6. By Lemma \ref{lem:mirror}, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace follows the same steps as ID, and hence also terminates in one of these steps.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.13
nodes.statement: According to Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace follow the same recursive trace. Thus, at any recursion level, both algorithms will stay at step $i \in [7]$. \textbf{Base case:} At recursion level $R=0$, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace start with the same input causal graph $G$. Thus, $G_{ID}= G_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace} = {\hat{{G}}} = G$. Also at $R=0$, the set of intervened variables ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}=\emptyset$. Thus, $G_{ID}= {\hat{{G}}} \setminus \emptyset = G$ holds. \textbf{Induction hypothesis:} At any recursion level $R=r$, let $G^{r}_{ID}$ be the graph parameter of the ID algorithm and $\{G^r_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r$, ${\hat{{G}}}^r\}$ be the parameters for the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm. We assume that $G^{r}_{ID}= G^{r}_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}$ and $G^{r}_{ID} = {\hat{{G}}}^r \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r$. \textbf{Inductive step:} The set of parameters $\{G_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}}\}$ of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and the graph parameter $G$ of ID are only updated at step 2 and step 7 for the next recursive calls. Thus, we prove the claim for these two steps separately. \textbf{At step 2}: In both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithms, we remove the non-ancestor variables $\mathbf{V}\setminus An(Y)$ from the graph. For ID, $G_{ID}^{r+1} = G_{ID}^r({An(\mathbf{Y})})$. For the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, we obtain $G_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}^{r+1} = G_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}^r({An(\mathbf{Y})})$. Thus, $G^{r+1}_{ID}=G^{r+1}_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}$. In \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, we also update ${\hat{{G}}}^{r+1}$ as ${\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r}({An(\mathbf{Y})})$. Since removing non-ancestor does not affect the intervened variables ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ anyway, the same relation between $G^{r+1}_{ID}$ and ${\hat{{G}}}^{r+1}$ is maintained, i.e., $G^{r+1}_{ID}= {\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$. \textbf{At step 7}: Both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace finds $\mathbf{X}_Z = \mathbf{X}\setminus S'$ and apply $\text{do}(\mathbf{X}_Z)$ as intervention. Also, in \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}$ is set to ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r \cup \mathbf{X}_Z$. \emph{For \text{ID-GEN}\xspace:} Since $\mathbf{X}_Z$ is intervened on, $G^r$ for \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is updated as $G^{r+1} = G^{r}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}_Z}}$ and ${\hat{{G}}}^r$ is updated as ${\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}_Z}}$. Now, $\mathbf{X}_Z$ has all incoming edges are cut off in $G^{r+1}$ and does not have any parents. As a result, removing $\mathbf{X}_Z$ from $G^{r+1}$ is valid. Thus, we obtain $G^{r+1} = G^{r+1} \setminus {\mathbf{X}_Z} = G^{r}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}_Z}} \setminus {\mathbf{X}_Z} $ $=G^r_{S'}$. However, for the other graph parameter, we keep ${\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}_Z}}$ as it is, since we would follow this structure in the base cases and consider $\mathbf{X}_Z$ while training the conditional models. Note that, in ${\hat{{G}}}^{r}$ the intervened variables ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r$ (before recursion level $r$) had already incoming edges removed. Thus, after ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r}$ being updated as ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r \cup \mathbf{X}_Z$, we can write ${\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}_Z}} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r}_{\overline{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}}}$. Since by inductive assumption, $G^{r} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r} \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r$, thus \begin{equation} G^{r+1} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} \setminus \{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r\cup \mathbf{X}_Z\}= {\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} \setminus \{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}\} \end{equation} \emph{For ID:} ID algorithm updates its parameters $G$ as $G^{r+1} = G^r_{S'}= G^r\setminus \mathbf{X}_Z$. Since \text{ID-GEN}\xspace and ID have the same graph parameter at recursion level $r$, i.e, $G^{r}_{ID}= G^{r}_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}$ and they updated the parameter in the same way, $G^{r+1}_{ID}=G^{r+1}_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}$ holds true. Since $G^{r+1}_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} \setminus \{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}\}$ according to Equation~\ref{eq:gr-ghatr}, we also obtain $G^{r+1}_{ID} = {\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} \setminus \{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}\}$. Therefore, the lemma holds for any recursion level $R$.

Since removing non-ancestor does not affect the intervened variables ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ anyway, the same relation between $G^{r+1}_{ID}$ and ${\hat{{G}}}^{r+1}$ is maintained, i.e., $G^{r+1}_{ID}= {\hat{{G}}}^{r+1} \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$. \textbf{At step 7}: Both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace finds $\mathbf{X}_Z = \mathbf{X}\setminus S'$ and apply $\text{do}(\mathbf{X}_Z)$ as intervention. Now, $\mathbf{X}_Z$ has all incoming edges are cut off in $G^{r+1}$ and does not have any parents. As a result, removing $\mathbf{X}_Z$ from $G^{r+1}$ is valid. Thus, we obtain $G^{r+1} = G^{r+1} \setminus {\mathbf{X}_Z} = G^{r}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}_Z}} \setminus {\mathbf{X}_Z} $ $=G^r_{S'}$. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.14
nodes.statement: According to Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace follow the same recursive trace. Thus, at any recursion level, both algorithms will stay at step $i \in [7]$. \textbf{Base case:} At recursion level $R=0$, ID starts with the observational distribution $P$ and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace starts with the observational training dataset $\mathcal{D} \sim P$. At $R=0$, ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= \emptyset$ since no variables have yet been intervened on. Thus, for ID algorithm $P_{ID} = P_{\emptyset} (V)$ holds. For \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, $\mathcal{D}[\emptyset, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{\emptyset}(\emptyset, \mathbf{V})$ holds. Thus, the claim is true for $R=0$. \textbf{Induction hypothesis:} Let the set of variables intervened at step 7s from the recursion level $R=0$ to $R=r$, be ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r$. At $R=r$, let the distribution parameter of the ID algorithm be $P^{r}_{ID}= P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(\mathbf{v})$. Let the dataset parameter of the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm be sampled from $P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{v})$, i.e, $\mathcal{D}^r \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{v})$. \textbf{Inductive step:} The distribution parameter $P$ of ID and the dataset parameter $\mathcal{D}$ of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace only change at step 2 and step 7 for the next recursive calls. Thus, we prove the claim for these two steps separately. \textbf{At step 2}: At step 2 of both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithms, there is no change in ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$, i.e., no additional variables are intervened to change the distribution $P$ or the dataset $\mathcal{D}$. At this step, we marginalize over $\mathbf{V}\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})$. Since ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \subset An(\mathbf{Y})_{{\hat{{G}}}}$, marginalizing non-ancestors out does not impact ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$. Thus, $P^{r+1}_{ID}(An(\mathbf{Y})) = \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G}P^{r}_{ID}(\mathbf{v}) = \sum_{\mathbf{V} \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G} P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(\mathbf{v}) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(An(\mathbf{Y})) $. This holds true since we can marginalize over $\mathbf{V} \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G$ in the joint interventional distribution. In the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, we drop the values of variables $\mathbf{V} \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G$ from the data set, that is, $\mathcal{D}^{r}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \rightarrow \mathcal{D}^{r+1}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, An(\mathbf{Y})_G].$ Since we assumed $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{v})$, therefore $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, An(\mathbf{Y})_G] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(An(\mathbf{Y}))$ holds. \textbf{At step 7}: At step 7, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm intervened on variable set $\mathbf{X}_Z$ where $\mathbf{X}_Z = \mathbf{X}\setminus S'$. Thus, at level $R=r+1$, we have ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r \cup \mathbf{X}_Z$. {Note that at this step, $S' = \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}_Z.$} ID algorithm updates its current distribution parameter $P^r_{ID}$ by intervening on $\mathbf{X}_Z$. Thus, at level $R=r+1$, $P^{r+1}_{ID}(\mathbf{v}\setminus \mathbf{x}_Z) = P^{r+1}_{ID}(s')= P^r_{ID}(\mathbf{v}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}_Z)) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(\mathbf{v}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}_Z)) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r \cup \mathbf{x}_Z}(s') = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}}(s').$ Thus the claim holds for ID algorithm at level $R=r+1$. In the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, we generate an interventional dataset $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[\mathbf{X}_Z, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S']$ by applying the $\text{do}(\mathbf{X}_Z)$ intervention on dataset $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$. Since $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{v})$, we obtain $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[\mathbf{X}_Z, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r, S']\sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r \cup \mathbf{x}_z}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{x}_z, s')$ $\implies \mathcal{D}^{r+1}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}, S']\sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}, s')$. Thus, the claim holds true for \text{ID-GEN}\xspace at the recursion level $R=r+1$. Therefore, $P(.)$ being the input distribution for ID and $\mathcal{D} \sim P(.)$ being the input dataset for \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, we proved by induction that $P_{ID} = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ and $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ at any recursion level.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the recursion level; only steps 2 (marginalization) and 7 (intervention on $X_Z$) change the distribution or the dataset.

nodes.name: ID-GEN drops columns
nodes.statement: In the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, we drop the values of variables $\mathbf{V} \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G$ from the data set, that is, $\mathcal{D}^{r}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \rightarrow \mathcal{D}^{r+1}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, An(\mathbf{Y})_G].$ Since we assumed $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{v})$, therefore $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, An(\mathbf{Y})_G] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(An(\mathbf{Y}))$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Dropping non-ancestor columns gives samples of $P_{\hat x^r}(An(Y))$.

nodes.name: At step 7
nodes.statement: \textbf{At step 7}: At step 7, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm intervened on variable set $\mathbf{X}_Z$ where $\mathbf{X}_Z = \mathbf{X}\setminus S'$. Thus, at level $R=r+1$, we have ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r \cup \mathbf{X}_Z$. {Note that at this step, $S' = \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}_Z.$} ID algorithm updates its current distribution parameter $P^r_{ID}$ by intervening on $\mathbf{X}_Z$. Thus, at level $R=r+1$, $P^{r+1}_{ID}(\mathbf{v}\setminus \mathbf{x}_Z) = P^{r+1}_{ID}(s')= P^r_{ID}(\mathbf{v}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}_Z)) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(\mathbf{v}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}_Z)) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r \cup \mathbf{x}_Z}(s') = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}}(s').$ Thus the claim holds for ID algorithm at level $R=r+1$. In the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, we generate an interventional dataset $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[\mathbf{X}_Z, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S']$ by applying the $\text{do}(\mathbf{X}_Z)$ intervention on dataset $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$. Since $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{v})$, we obtain $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[\mathbf{X}_Z, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r, S']\sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r \cup \mathbf{x}_z}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{x}_z, s')$ $\implies \mathcal{D}^{r+1}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}, S']\sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}, s')$. Thus, the claim holds true for \text{ID-GEN}\xspace at the recursion level $R=r+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Intervening on $X_Z$ preserves the claim.

nodes.name: Intervention set grows
nodes.statement: \textbf{At step 7}: At step 7, both ID and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm intervened on variable set $\mathbf{X}_Z$ where $\mathbf{X}_Z = \mathbf{X}\setminus S'$. Thus, at level $R=r+1$, we have ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1} = {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r \cup \mathbf{X}_Z$. {Note that at this step, $S' = \mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}_Z.$}
nodes.statement_short: $\hat X^{r+1}=\hat X^r\cup X_Z$.

nodes.name: ID side
nodes.statement: ID algorithm updates its current distribution parameter $P^r_{ID}$ by intervening on $\mathbf{X}_Z$. Thus, at level $R=r+1$, $P^{r+1}_{ID}(\mathbf{v}\setminus \mathbf{x}_Z) = P^{r+1}_{ID}(s')= P^r_{ID}(\mathbf{v}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}_Z)) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}(\mathbf{v}|\text{do}(\mathbf{x}_Z)) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r \cup \mathbf{x}_Z}(s') = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}}(s').$ Thus the claim holds for ID algorithm at level $R=r+1$.
nodes.statement_short: ID's distribution becomes $P_{\hat x^{r+1}}(s')$.

nodes.name: ID-GEN side
nodes.statement: In the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, we generate an interventional dataset $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[\mathbf{X}_Z, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S']$ by applying the $\text{do}(\mathbf{X}_Z)$ intervention on dataset $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$. Since $\mathcal{D}^r[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{v})$, we obtain $\mathcal{D}^{r+1}[\mathbf{X}_Z, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^r, S']\sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r \cup \mathbf{x}_z}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^r, \mathbf{x}_z, s')$ $\implies \mathcal{D}^{r+1}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}^{r+1}, S']\sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{r+1}, s')$. Thus, the claim holds true for \text{ID-GEN}\xspace at the recursion level $R=r+1$.
nodes.statement_short: The generated dataset is sampled from $P_{\hat x^{r+1}}(\hat x^{r+1}, s')$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, $P(.)$ being the input distribution for ID and $\mathcal{D} \sim P(.)$ being the input dataset for \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, we proved by induction that $P_{ID} = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ and $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ at any recursion level.
nodes.statement_short: By induction the claim holds at every level.

nodes.name: ID distribution equals ID-GEN conditional distribution
nodes.statement: Consider recursive calls $ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, P_{ID}(\mathbf{v}))$ and \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace at any recursion level $R$. If $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, V] \sim P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$, then$P_{ID}(\mathbf{v}) = P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ for fixed values of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$.
assumptions: $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, V] \sim P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$
conclusions: $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v}) = P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ for fixed values of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$
nodes.label: lem:same-dist-graph

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.15
nodes.statement: At any level $R=r$ of the recursion , we have $G_{ID} = G_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}$ and $G_{ID}= {\hat{{G}}} \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dag-dag} and $P_{ID} = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ and $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-dist} where $P(\mathbf{v})$ is the input observational distribution. Let $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}) = P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}), \forall {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$. Now, since in ${\hat{{G}}}$ we have already intervened on ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$, for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, we have $P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) *P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$, thus $\mathbf{V}$ will be sampled from $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ for fixed consistent ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$. On the other hand, in the ID algorithm, at any recursion level, $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v}) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ for fixed consistent ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ and $G_{ID}= {\hat{{G}}} \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$. Since according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-dist}, $P_{ID} = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ and $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ at any recursion level, i.e., starting from the same $P(\mathbf{V})$, the same set of interventions are performed in the same manner in both algorithms; thus for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, we obtain $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ .
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemmas D.13 and D.14 and condition on the intervened values $\hat x$.

nodes.name: Recall Lemmas D.13, D.14
nodes.statement: At any level $R=r$ of the recursion , we have $G_{ID} = G_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}$ and $G_{ID}= {\hat{{G}}} \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dag-dag} and $P_{ID} = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ and $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-dist} where $P(\mathbf{v})$ is the input observational distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the graph and distribution relations of Lemmas D.13 and D.14.

nodes.name: ID-GEN side
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}) = P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}), \forall {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$. Now, since in ${\hat{{G}}}$ we have already intervened on ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$, for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, we have $P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) *P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$, thus $\mathbf{V}$ will be sampled from $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ for fixed consistent ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\hat X$ is intervened on, $V$ is sampled from $P_{ID-GEN}(v|\hat x)$.

nodes.name: ID side
nodes.statement: On the other hand, in the ID algorithm, at any recursion level, $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v}) = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ for fixed consistent ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ and $G_{ID}= {\hat{{G}}} \setminus {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: ID's distribution is $P_{\hat x}(v)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-dist}, $P_{ID} = P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{v})$ and $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ at any recursion level, i.e., starting from the same $P(\mathbf{V})$, the same set of interventions are performed in the same manner in both algorithms; thus for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, we obtain $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ .
nodes.statement_short: Same interventions applied the same way give $P_{ID}(v)=P_{ID-GEN}(v|\hat x)$.

nodes.name: ID-GEN fails on non-identifiable queries
nodes.statement: If a non-identifiable query is passed to it, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace will return \texttt{FAIL}.
assumptions: a non-identifiable query is passed to it
conclusions: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace will return \texttt{FAIL}
nodes.label: lem:fail

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.16
nodes.statement: Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is given a non-identifiable query as input. Since the ID algorithm is complete, if ID is given this query, it will reach its step 5 and return \texttt{FAIL}. According to the lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace follows the same trace and the same sequence of steps as ID for a fixed input. Since for the non-identifiable query ID reaches step 5, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace will also reach step 5 and return \texttt{FAIL}.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer from ID: completeness of ID and the shared trace force step 5.

nodes.name: ID reaches step 5
nodes.statement: Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is given a non-identifiable query as input. Since the ID algorithm is complete, if ID is given this query, it will reach its step 5 and return \texttt{FAIL}.
nodes.statement_short: By completeness, ID reaches step 5 and fails on this query.

nodes.name: Same trace
nodes.statement: According to the lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace follows the same trace and the same sequence of steps as ID for a fixed input.
nodes.statement_short: ID-GEN follows ID's trace (Lemma D.11).

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since for the non-identifiable query ID reaches step 5, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace will also reach step 5 and return \texttt{FAIL}.
nodes.statement_short: So ID-GEN also reaches step 5 and returns FAIL.

nodes.name: ID-GEN base case (step 1)
nodes.statement: \textbf{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace Base case (step 1):} Let, at any recursion level of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, the input dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$ is sampled from a specific joint distribution $P({\hat{\mathbf{X}}},\mathbf{V})$, i.e., $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P({\hat{\mathbf{X}}},\mathbf{V})$ where ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ is the set of intervened variables at step 7s. Given a target interventional query $P(\mathbf{y})$ over a causal graph $G=(V, E)$, suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}= \emptyset, G, \mathcal{D}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$ enters step 1 and returns $\mathcal{H}$. Then $\mathcal{H}$ is a valid sampling network for $P(\mathbf{y})$ with fixed consistent ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$.
assumptions: at any recursion level of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, the input dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$ is sampled from a specific joint distribution $P({\hat{\mathbf{X}}},\mathbf{V})$
suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}= \emptyset, G, \mathcal{D}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$ enters step 1 and returns $\mathcal{H}$
conclusions: $\mathcal{H}$ is a valid sampling network for $P(\mathbf{y})$  with fixed consistent ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$
nodes.statement_short: The sampling network returned at step 1 is valid for $P(y)$ once $\hat X$ is fixed.
nodes.label: lem:step1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.17
nodes.statement: Since the intervention set $\mathbf{X}$ is empty, we are at the base case step 1 of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace. Suppose that for the same query, the ID algorithm reaches step 1. Let $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})$ be the current distribution of the ID algorithm after performing a series of marginalizations in step 2 and intervention in step 7 on the input observational distribution. $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$ is the dataset parameter of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm that went through the same transformations as the ID algorithm in the sample space according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}. ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ is the set of interventions that are applied on the dataset at step 7s. Since ID algorithm is sound it returns correct output for the query $P(\mathbf{y})$. We prove the soundness of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace step 1 by showing that the sampling network \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns, is valid for the output of the ID algorithm. ID algorithm is sound and factorizes $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})$ with respect to the graph $G$ as below. \begin{equation*} P_{ID}(\mathbf{v}) = \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}) \end{equation*} And obtains $ P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})$ by: \begin{equation} P_{ID}(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{v\setminus y} \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}) \end{equation} Let $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}) = P({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}), \forall ({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$. For fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ can be factorized with respect to $G$ and ${\hat{{G}}}$ as following: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) &= \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}, {\hat{\mathbf{x}}})\\ &= \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}) \\ \text{\hspace{5mm} [Changed the graph from $G$ to ${\hat{{G}}}$} & \text{ since ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \in {\hat{{G}}}$ and only affects the descendants of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$.]} \end{split} \end{equation*} And $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ can be obtained by: \begin{equation} P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) = \sum_{v\setminus y} \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}) \end{equation} Since for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} ={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}. Thus, the corresponding conditional distributions in Equation~\ref{eq:step1-id-factor} and ~\ref{eq:step1-iddag-factor} are equal, i.e, $P_{ID}(v_i | v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}) = P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}), \forall \{i|V_i\in \mathbf{V}\}$. Therefore, $P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})$ and $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ having the same factorization and the corresponding conditional distributions being equal implies that $P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$. Now, based on Assumption~\ref{assum:correct_cond}, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace learns to sample from each conditional distribution $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(v_i| v_{\pi}^{(i-1)}, v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)})$ of the product in Equation~\ref{eq:step1-iddag-factor}, by training a conditional model $M_{V_i}$ on samples from the dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]\sim {P({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})}$. For each $V_i$, we add a node containing $V_i$ and its associated conditional generative model $M_{V_i}$ to a sampling network. This produces a sampling network $\mathcal{H}$ that is a DAG, where each variable $V_i \in \mathbf{V}$ has a sampling mechanism. By factorization and Assumption~\ref{assum:correct_cond}, ancestral sampling from this sampling graph produces samples from $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$. We can drop values of $V\setminus Y$ to obtain the samples from $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$. Since $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$, both factorized in the same manner and $M_{V_i}$ learned conditional distribution of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace's factorization, the sampling network returned by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, will correctly sample from the distribution $P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})$ returned by the ID algorithm for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$. Thus, the sampling network returned by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is valid for $P(\mathbf{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare ID's step-1 factorization with ID-GEN's factorization over $\hat G$; by Lemma D.15 the conditionals coincide. Correct conditional models (Assumption D.5) then make ancestral sampling exact.

nodes.name: Both at step 1
nodes.statement: Since the intervention set $\mathbf{X}$ is empty, we are at the base case step 1 of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace. Suppose that for the same query, the ID algorithm reaches step 1.
nodes.statement_short: Both algorithms are at step 1 for the same query.

nodes.name: Current distribution and dataset
nodes.statement: Let $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})$ be the current distribution of the ID algorithm after performing a series of marginalizations in step 2 and intervention in step 7 on the input observational distribution. $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$ is the dataset parameter of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm that went through the same transformations as the ID algorithm in the sample space according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}. ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ is the set of interventions that are applied on the dataset at step 7s.
nodes.statement_short: Let $P_{ID}(v)$ be ID's current distribution and $D[\hat X, V]$ ID-GEN's dataset (Lemma D.15).

nodes.name: Reduce to validity for ID's output
nodes.statement: Since ID algorithm is sound it returns correct output for the query $P(\mathbf{y})$. We prove the soundness of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace step 1 by showing that the sampling network \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns, is valid for the output of the ID algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show the network is valid for ID's (correct) output.

nodes.name: ID factorization
nodes.statement: ID algorithm is sound and factorizes $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})$ with respect to the graph $G$ as below. \begin{equation*} P_{ID}(\mathbf{v}) = \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}) \end{equation*} And obtains $ P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})$ by: \begin{equation} P_{ID}(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{v\setminus y} \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: ID factorizes $P_{ID}(y)$ as a marginalized topological product (eq. 3).

nodes.name: ID-GEN factorization
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}) = P({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v}), \forall ({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$. For fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ can be factorized with respect to $G$ and ${\hat{{G}}}$ as following: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) &= \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}, {\hat{\mathbf{x}}})\\ &= \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}) \\ \text{\hspace{5mm} [Changed the graph from $G$ to ${\hat{{G}}}$} & \text{ since ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \in {\hat{{G}}}$ and only affects the descendants of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$.]} \end{split} \end{equation*} And $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ can be obtained by: \begin{equation} P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) = \sum_{v\setminus y} \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: ID-GEN's conditional factorizes the same way over $\hat G$ (eq. 4).

nodes.name: Conditionals coincide
nodes.statement: Since for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} ={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}. Thus, the corresponding conditional distributions in Equation~\ref{eq:step1-id-factor} and ~\ref{eq:step1-iddag-factor} are equal, i.e, $P_{ID}(v_i | v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}) = P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}), \forall \{i|V_i\in \mathbf{V}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma D.15 the corresponding conditional factors are equal.

nodes.name: Target distributions coincide
nodes.statement: Therefore, $P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})$ and $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ having the same factorization and the corresponding conditional distributions being equal implies that $P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $P_{ID}(y)=P_{ID-GEN}(y|\hat x)$.

nodes.name: Models learn the factors
nodes.statement: Now, based on Assumption~\ref{assum:correct_cond}, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace learns to sample from each conditional distribution $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(v_i| v_{\pi}^{(i-1)}, v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)})$ of the product in Equation~\ref{eq:step1-iddag-factor}, by training a conditional model $M_{V_i}$ on samples from the dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]\sim {P({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Assumption D.5 each trained model samples its conditional factor.

nodes.name: Build the DAG network
nodes.statement: For each $V_i$, we add a node containing $V_i$ and its associated conditional generative model $M_{V_i}$ to a sampling network. This produces a sampling network $\mathcal{H}$ that is a DAG, where each variable $V_i \in \mathbf{V}$ has a sampling mechanism.
nodes.statement_short: Wire the models into a DAG sampling network.

nodes.name: Network is valid
nodes.statement: By factorization and Assumption~\ref{assum:correct_cond}, ancestral sampling from this sampling graph produces samples from $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$. We can drop values of $V\setminus Y$ to obtain the samples from $P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$. Since $P_{ID}(\mathbf{v})= P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$, both factorized in the same manner and $M_{V_i}$ learned conditional distribution of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace's factorization, the sampling network returned by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, will correctly sample from the distribution $P_{ID}(\mathbf{y})$ returned by the ID algorithm for fixed ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$. Thus, the sampling network returned by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is valid for $P(\mathbf{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Ancestral sampling and dropping $V\setminus Y$ gives samples of $P_{ID}(y)$: the network is valid.

nodes.name: ID step-1 factorization
nodes.statement: P_{ID}(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{v\setminus y} \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)})
nodes.label: eq:step1-id-factor

nodes.name: ID-GEN step-1 factorization
nodes.statement: P_{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) = \sum_{v\setminus y} \prod_{v_i\in V} P(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)})
nodes.label: eq:step1-iddag-factor

nodes.name: ID-GEN base case (step 6)
nodes.statement: \textbf{\text{ID-GEN}\xspace Base case (step 6):} Let, at any recursion level of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, the input dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]$ is sampled from a specific joint distribution $P({\hat{\mathbf{X}}},\mathbf{V})$, i.e., $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P({\hat{\mathbf{X}}},\mathbf{V})$ where ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ is the set of intervened variables at step 7s. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.18
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:mirror}, both \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace and $ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enter the same base case step $6$. By the condition of step $6$, $G\setminus \mathbf{X}$ has only one c-component $\{S\}$, where $S\in C(G)$. Let $P(\mathbf{v})$ be the current distribution of the ID algorithm after performing a series of marginalizations in step 2 and intervention in step 7 on the input observational distribution. Let $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}] \sim P'({\hat{\mathbf{x}}},\mathbf{v})$ be the dataset parameter of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm that went through the same transformations as the ID algorithm in the sample space. ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ is the set of interventions that are applied on the dataset at step 7s. According to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph} for fixed values of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $P(\mathbf{v}) = P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ holds true at any recursion level. Since ID algorithm is sound it returns correct output for the query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$. We prove the soundness of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace step 6 by showing that the sampling network \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns, is valid for the output of the ID algorithm. With the joint distribution $P(\mathbf{v})$, the soundness of ID implies that \begin{equation} P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})= \sum_{S\setminus Y}\prod_{\{i\mid V_i\in S\}}P(v_i| v_{\pi_G}^{(i-1)}) \end{equation} where $\pi_G$ is a topological ordering for $G$. With the joint distribution $P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace can factorize $P'_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})$ in the same manner: \begin{equation} \begin{split} P'_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})&= \sum_{S\setminus Y}\prod_{\{i\mid V_i\in S\}}P'(v_i| v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}, {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) \\ &= \sum_{S\setminus Y}\prod_{\{i\mid V_i\in S\}}P'(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}) \\ \text{\hspace{5mm} [Changed the graph from $G$ to ${\hat{{G}}}$} & \text{ since ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \in {\hat{{G}}}$ and only affects the descendants of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$.]} \end{split} \end{equation} Since $P(\mathbf{v}) = P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$, the corresponding conditional distributions in Equation~\ref{eq:step6-id-factor} and ~\ref{eq:step6-iddag-factor} are equal, i.e, $P(v_i | v_{\pi_{G}}^{(i-1)}) = P'(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}), \forall \{i|V_i\in S\}$. Therefore, $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ and $P'_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ having the same factorization and the corresponding conditional distributions being equal implies that $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = P'_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace operates in this case by training, from joint samples $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, V]$, a model to correctly sample each $P'(v_i \mid v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)})$ term, i.e., we learn a conditional generative model $M_{V_i}(V_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)})$ which produces samples from $P'(v_i \mid v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)})$, which we can do according to Assumption~\ref{assum:correct_cond}. Then we construct a sampling network $\mathcal{H}$ by creating a node $V_i$ with a sampling mechanism $M_{V_i}$ for each $V_i \in S$. We add edges from $V_j\to V_i$ for each $V_j\in V_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)}$. Since every vertex in ${\hat{{G}}}$ is either in $S$ or in $\mathbf{X} \cup {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$, every edge either connects to a previously constructed node or a variable in $\mathbf{X} \cup {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$. Since we already have fixed values for ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, when we specify values for $\mathbf{X}$ and sample according to topological order $\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}$, this sampling graph provides samples from the distribution $\prod_{\{i\mid V_i\in S\}}P'(v_i| v_{\pi_{{\hat{{G}}}}}^{(i-1)})$, i.e. $P'_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{s}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$. Since, as shown earlier, $P'_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{s}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) = P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{s})$, samples from the sampling network $\mathcal{H}$ is consistent with $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{s})$ as well. We obtain samples from $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ by dropping the values of $S\setminus Y$ from the samples obtained from $ P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{s})$. We assert the remaining conditions to show that this sampling network is correct for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$: certainly this graph is a $DAG$ and every $v\in S$ has a conditional generative model in $\mathcal{H}$. By the conditions to enter step 6, ${\hat{{G}}}=S\cup \mathbf{X} \cup {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ and $S\cap \{\mathbf{X} \cup {\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \}=\emptyset$. Then every node in $\mathcal{H}$ is either in $S$ or is in $\mathbf{X} \cup {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$: hence the only nodes without sampling mechanisms are those in $\mathbf{X} \cup {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ as desired. Therefore, when ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ is fixed as ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $\mathcal{H}$ is a valid sampling network for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}).$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.21
