nodes.name: Proof of ID-GEN soundness
nodes.statement_short: Structural induction over the recursion: base cases by Lemmas D.17 and D.18, and each recursive step (2, 3, 4, 7) mirrors ID's call on a correctly generated dataset. Step 4 merges the c-factor networks, which stay acyclic by Lemma D.20.

nodes.name: Base cases
nodes.statement: We proceed by structural induction. We start from the base cases, i.e., the steps that do not call \text{ID-GEN}\xspace again. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace only has three base cases: step 1 is the case when no variables are being intervened upon and is covered by Lemma \ref{lem:step1}; step 6 is the other base case and is covered by Lemma \ref{lem:step6}; step 5 is the non-identifiable case and since we assumed that $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is identifiable, we can skip \text{ID-GEN}\xspace's step 5.
nodes.statement_short: Structural induction; base cases steps 1 and 6 by Lemmas D.17 and D.18, step 5 excluded by identifiability.

nodes.name: Proof recipe
nodes.statement: The structure of our proof is as follows. By the assumption that $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is identifiable and due to Lemma \ref{lem:termination}, its recursions must terminate in steps 1 or 6. Since we have already proven correctness for these cases, we use these as base cases for a structural induction. We prove that if \text{ID-GEN}\xspace enters any of step 2, 3, 4 or 7, under the inductive assumption that we have correct sampling network for the recursive calls, we can produce a correct overall sampling network. The general flavor of these inductive steps adheres to the following recipe: i) determine the corresponding recursive call that ID algorithm makes; ii) argue that we can generate the correct dataset to be analogous to the distribution that ID uses in the recursion; iii) rely on the inductive assumption that the generated DAG from \text{ID-GEN}\xspace's recursion is correct.
nodes.statement_short: Recursions terminate in steps 1 or 6 (Lemma D.12); for steps 2, 3, 4, 7 mirror ID's call on a matching dataset.

nodes.name: Step 2
nodes.statement: We consider each recursive case separately. We start with step 2. Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 2, then according to Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, $ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 2 as well. Hence the correct distribution to sample from is provided by ID step 2: \[P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})= ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}\cap An(Y)_G, \sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G} P(\mathbf{v}), G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}).\] Now, according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}, at the current step, the dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is sampled from a distribution $P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ such that for fixed values of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $P(\mathbf{v}) = P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ holds true. Following our recipe, we need to update the dataset $\mathcal{D}$ such that it is sampled from $\sum_{V\setminus An(Y)_G} P(\mathbf{v}) =\sum_{V\setminus An(Y)_G} P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) $. We do this by dropping all non-ancestor variables of $\mathbf{Y}$ (in the graph $G$) from the dataset $\mathcal{D}$, thereby attaining samples from the joint distribution $\sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G} P(\mathbf{v})$. Since ${\hat{{G}}}$ is used at the base case, we update it as ${\hat{{G}}}_{An(\mathbf{Y})}$, the same as $G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}$ to propagate the correct graph at the next step. Therefore, we can generate the sampling network from $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap An(\mathbf{Y})_G, G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}, \mathcal{D}[An(Y)], {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}}_{An(Y)})$ by the inductive assumption and simply return it.
nodes.statement_short: Drop non-ancestors from the data and recurse.

nodes.name: Both enter step 2
nodes.statement: We consider each recursive case separately. We start with step 2. Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 2, then according to Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, $ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 2 as well.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma D.11 ID also enters step 2.

nodes.name: ID's step-2 target
nodes.statement: Hence the correct distribution to sample from is provided by ID step 2: \[P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})= ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}\cap An(Y)_G, \sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G} P(\mathbf{v}), G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}).\]
nodes.statement_short: The target is ID's recursive call on the ancestral marginal.

nodes.name: Dataset distribution
nodes.statement: Now, according to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}, at the current step, the dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is sampled from a distribution $P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ such that for fixed values of ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}={\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$, $P(\mathbf{v}) = P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}})$ holds true.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma D.15 the data come from $P'(v|\hat x)=P(v)$.

nodes.name: Required dataset
nodes.statement: Following our recipe, we need to update the dataset $\mathcal{D}$ such that it is sampled from $\sum_{V\setminus An(Y)_G} P(\mathbf{v}) =\sum_{V\setminus An(Y)_G} P'(\mathbf{v}|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}) $.
nodes.statement_short: The dataset must follow the ancestral marginal.

nodes.name: Drop non-ancestors and recurse
nodes.statement: We do this by dropping all non-ancestor variables of $\mathbf{Y}$ (in the graph $G$) from the dataset $\mathcal{D}$, thereby attaining samples from the joint distribution $\sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G} P(\mathbf{v})$. Since ${\hat{{G}}}$ is used at the base case, we update it as ${\hat{{G}}}_{An(\mathbf{Y})}$, the same as $G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}$ to propagate the correct graph at the next step. Therefore, we can generate the sampling network from $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap An(\mathbf{Y})_G, G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}, \mathcal{D}[An(Y)], {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}}_{An(Y)})$ by the inductive assumption and simply return it.
nodes.statement_short: Dropping non-ancestor columns gives it; recurse by the inductive assumption.

nodes.name: Step 3
nodes.statement: Next, we consider step 3. Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 3. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, $ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 3, and the correct distribution to sample from is provided from ID step 3 as \[ P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cup W, P, G) \] where $W:= (\mathbf{V}\setminus \mathbf{X})\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_{G_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}$. Since the distribution passed to the recursive call is $P$, we can simply return the sampling graph generated by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace, which we know is correct for $P_{\mathbf{X}\cup \mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{Y})$ by the inductive assumption. Thus, the returned sampling network by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace can sample from $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$. While we do need to specify a sampling mechanism for $\mathbf{W}$ to satisfy our definition of a valid sampling network, this can be chosen arbitrarily, say $\mathbf{W}\sim P(\mathbf{w})$ or uniform the distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Enlarge $X$ by $W$ and reuse the recursive network.

nodes.name: Both enter step 3
nodes.statement: Next, we consider step 3. Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 3. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, $ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 3, and the correct distribution to sample from is provided from ID step 3 as \[ P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cup W, P, G) \] where $W:= (\mathbf{V}\setminus \mathbf{X})\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_{G_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: ID enters step 3 too; the target is $ID(Y, X\cup W, P, G)$.

nodes.name: Return recursive network
nodes.statement: Since the distribution passed to the recursive call is $P$, we can simply return the sampling graph generated by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace, which we know is correct for $P_{\mathbf{X}\cup \mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{Y})$ by the inductive assumption. Thus, the returned sampling network by \text{ID-GEN}\xspace can sample from $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: The data are unchanged, so the recursive network is correct by induction.

nodes.name: Mechanism for W
nodes.statement: While we do need to specify a sampling mechanism for $\mathbf{W}$ to satisfy our definition of a valid sampling network, this can be chosen arbitrarily, say $\mathbf{W}\sim P(\mathbf{w})$ or uniform the distribution.
nodes.statement_short: $W$ may be given any sampling mechanism.

nodes.name: Step 4
nodes.statement: Next we consider step 4. Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 4. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, $ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 4 and the correct distribution to sample from is provided from ID step 4 as: \[ \sum_{V\setminus(y\cup x)}\prod_i ID(s_i, v\setminus s_i, P, G) \] where $S_i$ are the c-components of $G\setminus \mathbf{X}$, i.e., elements of $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})$. By the inductive assumption, we can sample from each term in the product with the sampling network returned by $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(S_{i}, \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V} \setminus S_{i}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$. However, recall the output of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns a `headless' (no conditional models for $\mathbf{X}$) sampling network as follows: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace returns a sampling network, i.e., a collection of conditional generative models where for each variable in $G$ and every variable except those in $\mathbf{X}$ have a specified conditional generative model. To sample from this sampling network, values for $\mathbf{X}$ must first be specified. In the step 4 case, the values $\mathbf{v} \setminus s_i$ need to be provided to sample values for $S_i$, and similarly for $i\neq j$, values $\mathbf{v} \setminus s_j$ are needed to sample values for $S_j$. Since $S_i\subseteq (\mathbf{V} \setminus S_j)$ and $S_j\subseteq (\mathbf{V} \setminus S_i)$, it might lead to cycles (as shown in Example~\ref{ex:cyclic}) if we attempt to generate samples for each c-components sequentially. Thus, it does not suffice to sample from each c-component sequentially or separately. Note that, $H_i$ is the correct sampling network corresponding to $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(S_{i}, \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V} \setminus S_{i}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$ by definition, for each node $V_i\in S_i$, $V_i$ has a conditional generative model in $H_i$. By Lemma \ref{lem:acyclic}, each edge in $H_i$ adheres to the topological ordering $\pi_G$ (at the current level). Hence, if we apply \texttt{MergeNetwork(.)}\xspace to construct a graph $\mathcal{H}$ from $\{H_i\}_i$, it will also adhere to the original topological ordering $\pi_G$. Thus, $\mathcal{H}$ is a DAG. Since every node $V_i$ in $G\setminus \mathbf{X}$ has a conditional generative model in some $H_i$, the only nodes in combined $\mathcal{H}$ without conditional generative models are those in $\mathbf{X}$. Finally, since each node in $\mathcal{H}$ samples the correct conditional distribution by the inductive assumption, $\mathcal{H}$ samples from the product distribution $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ corretly. The sum $\sum_{\mathbf{v}\setminus(\mathbf{y}\cup \mathbf{x})}$ can be safely ignored now and can be applied later since the sample values of the marginalized variables ($\mathbf{v}\setminus(\mathbf{y}\cup \mathbf{x})$) can be dropped from the joint at the end of the algorithm to attain samples values of the remaining variables. Hence $\mathcal{H}$ is correct for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Merge the c-factor networks into one acyclic network.

nodes.name: Both enter step 4
nodes.statement: Next we consider step 4. Suppose \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 4. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, $ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 4 and the correct distribution to sample from is provided from ID step 4 as: \[ \sum_{V\setminus(y\cup x)}\prod_i ID(s_i, v\setminus s_i, P, G) \] where $S_i$ are the c-components of $G\setminus \mathbf{X}$, i.e., elements of $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})$. By the inductive assumption, we can sample from each term in the product with the sampling network returned by $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(S_{i}, \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V} \setminus S_{i}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$. However, recall the output of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns a `headless' (no conditional models for $\mathbf{X}$) sampling network as follows:
nodes.statement_short: ID enters step 4; each c-factor is sampled by its recursive network.

nodes.name: Headless networks may cycle
nodes.statement: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace returns a sampling network, i.e., a collection of conditional generative models where for each variable in $G$ and every variable except those in $\mathbf{X}$ have a specified conditional generative model. To sample from this sampling network, values for $\mathbf{X}$ must first be specified. In the step 4 case, the values $\mathbf{v} \setminus s_i$ need to be provided to sample values for $S_i$, and similarly for $i\neq j$, values $\mathbf{v} \setminus s_j$ are needed to sample values for $S_j$. Since $S_i\subseteq (\mathbf{V} \setminus S_j)$ and $S_j\subseteq (\mathbf{V} \setminus S_i)$, it might lead to cycles (as shown in Example~\ref{ex:cyclic}) if we attempt to generate samples for each c-components sequentially. Thus, it does not suffice to sample from each c-component sequentially or separately.
nodes.statement_short: Networks need values of $V\setminus S_i$, so sampling c-components separately can deadlock (Example C.1).

nodes.name: Merged network is a DAG
nodes.statement: Note that, $H_i$ is the correct sampling network corresponding to $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(S_{i}, \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V} \setminus S_{i}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$ by definition, for each node $V_i\in S_i$, $V_i$ has a conditional generative model in $H_i$. By Lemma \ref{lem:acyclic}, each edge in $H_i$ adheres to the topological ordering $\pi_G$ (at the current level). Hence, if we apply \texttt{MergeNetwork(.)}\xspace to construct a graph $\mathcal{H}$ from $\{H_i\}_i$, it will also adhere to the original topological ordering $\pi_G$. Thus, $\mathcal{H}$ is a DAG.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma D.20 all $H_i$ respect $\pi_G$, so the merged $\mathcal{H}$ is a DAG.

nodes.name: Merged network is correct
nodes.statement: Since every node $V_i$ in $G\setminus \mathbf{X}$ has a conditional generative model in some $H_i$, the only nodes in combined $\mathcal{H}$ without conditional generative models are those in $\mathbf{X}$. Finally, since each node in $\mathcal{H}$ samples the correct conditional distribution by the inductive assumption, $\mathcal{H}$ samples from the product distribution $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ corretly. The sum $\sum_{\mathbf{v}\setminus(\mathbf{y}\cup \mathbf{x})}$ can be safely ignored now and can be applied later since the sample values of the marginalized variables ($\mathbf{v}\setminus(\mathbf{y}\cup \mathbf{x})$) can be dropped from the joint at the end of the algorithm to attain samples values of the remaining variables. Hence $\mathcal{H}$ is correct for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Only $X$ lacks models and each node samples correctly, so $\mathcal{H}$ is correct for $P_x(y)$.

nodes.name: Steps 5 and 6
nodes.statement: Step 5 can never happen by the assumption that $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is identifiable, and step 6 has already been covered as a base case. The only step remaining is step 7. \begin{figure}[omitted: a diagram of this paper's results, not reproduced here]\end{figure}
nodes.statement_short: Step 5 cannot occur and step 6 is a base case; step 7 remains.

nodes.name: Step 7
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror} says, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 7 by the same conditions $ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 7. Then by assumption, $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and there exists a confounding component $S'\in C(G)$ such that $S\subset S'$. The correct distribution to sample from is provided from ID step 7 as \[ P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap S', P', G_{S'}) \] where \[P' := \prod_{\{i|V_i\in S'\}} P(V_i| V_\pi^{(i-1)}\cap S', v_\pi^{(i-1)}\setminus S').\] Examining ID algorithm more closely, if we enter step 7 during ID, the interventional set $\mathbf{X}$ is partitioned into two components: $\mathbf{X}\cap S'$ and $\mathbf{X}_Z:=\mathbf{X}\setminus S'$. From Lemmas 33 and 37 of \citet{shpitser2008complete}, in the event we enter step 7, $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is equivalent to $P'_{\mathbf{x} \cap S'}(\mathbf{y})$ where $P'(\mathbf{v})=P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}(\mathbf{v})$. ID estimates $P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}(\mathbf{v})$ with a similar computation as the step 6 base case. To sample correctly in \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, we consider two cases.\\ i) ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}=\emptyset$: When \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step 7 for the first time, we have ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}=\emptyset$. In that case, we first update our dataset $\mathcal{D}[\mathbf{V}]\sim P(\mathbf{v})$ to samples from $\mathcal{D}'\sim P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}( \mathbf{v})$, and then we recurse on the query $P'_{\mathbf{x}\cap S'}(\mathbf{y})$ over the graph $G_{S'}$. Also, $\mathbf{X}_Z$ is outside the c-component $S'$. Therefore we generate a dataset from $\mathcal{D}'\sim P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}(S')$ via running directly the $\texttt{ConditionalGMs(.)}\xspace$ of the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, Algorithm~\ref{alg:step1}: $\texttt{ConditionalGMs}(S', X_Z, G, \mathcal{D}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$. This is attainable via the inductive assumption and Lemma \ref{lem:termination}. The only divergence from ID during the generation of $\mathcal{D}'$ is that ID presumes pre-specified fixed values for $\mathbf{X}_Z$, where we train a sampling mechanism that is agnostic a priori to the specific choice of $\mathbf{X}_Z$. To sidestep this issue, we generate a dataset with all possible values of $\mathbf{X}_Z$ and be sure to record the values of $\mathbf{X}_Z$ in the dataset $\mathcal{D}'[\mathbf{X}_Z, S']$. ii) ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \neq \emptyset$: When \text{ID-GEN}\xspace has visited step 7 already once and thus ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}\neq \emptyset$. We consider ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ along with $\mathbf{X}_Z$ when generating $\mathcal{D}'$ this time. More precisely, we update our dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]\sim P({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ to samples from $\mathcal{D}'\sim P_{\mathbf{x}_Z \cup {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{x}_z, {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$. Rest of the steps follow similarly as the above case. We record the new $\mathbf{X}_Z$ in ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ and carry them in $\mathcal{D}'[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S']$ and ${\hat{{G}}}$. Next, we need to map the recursive call $ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap S', P', G)$ to \text{ID-GEN}\xspace. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace sends the same parameters $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap S'$ and $G$ as ID. Now, equivalent to passing the distribution $P'$ of ID, we pass the dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S']$ sampled from this distribution, including the intervened values for ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ used to obtain this dataset. According to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}, this dataset is sampled from $P'$ if we fix to a specific value ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$. Finally, ID algorithm uses specific value of $\mathbf{X}_Z$ and then ignores those variables from $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$ for rest of the recursion. On the other hand, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace saves $\mathbf{X}_Z$ in ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ as ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \cup \mathbf{X}_Z$ and keeps ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ connected to ${\hat{{G}}}$ with incoming edges cut, i.e., $G_{S',\overline{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}}$ for the next recursive calls since \text{ID-GEN}\xspace utilizes ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ and the topological order in ${\hat{{G}}}$ at the base cases (step 1 and 6). By the inductive assumption, we can generate a correct sampling network from the call $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X} \setminus \mathbf{X}_Z , G_{S'}, \mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S], {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}}_{\{S', \overline{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}\}} $), and hence the returned sampling graph is correct for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}).$
nodes.statement_short: Generate a do($X_Z$) dataset and recurse on $G_{S'}$.

nodes.name: Both enter step 7
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:mirror} says, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace$(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, G, \mathcal{D}, {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$\xspace enters step 7 by the same conditions $ID(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X}, P, G)$ enters step 7. Then by assumption, $C(G\setminus \mathbf{X})=\{S\}$ and there exists a confounding component $S'\in C(G)$ such that $S\subset S'$. The correct distribution to sample from is provided from ID step 7 as \[ P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) = ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap S', P', G_{S'}) \] where \[P' := \prod_{\{i|V_i\in S'\}} P(V_i| V_\pi^{(i-1)}\cap S', v_\pi^{(i-1)}\setminus S').\]
nodes.statement_short: ID enters step 7 and recurses with $P'$ on $G_{S'}$.

nodes.name: Shpitser-Pearl reduction
nodes.statement: Examining ID algorithm more closely, if we enter step 7 during ID, the interventional set $\mathbf{X}$ is partitioned into two components: $\mathbf{X}\cap S'$ and $\mathbf{X}_Z:=\mathbf{X}\setminus S'$. From Lemmas 33 and 37 of \citet{shpitser2008complete}, in the event we enter step 7, $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is equivalent to $P'_{\mathbf{x} \cap S'}(\mathbf{y})$ where $P'(\mathbf{v})=P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}(\mathbf{v})$. ID estimates $P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}(\mathbf{v})$ with a similar computation as the step 6 base case.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemmas 33 and 37 of Shpitser and Pearl, $P_x(y)=P'_{x\cap S'}(y)$ with $P'=P_{x_Z}$.

nodes.name: Case: X-hat empty
nodes.statement: To sample correctly in \text{ID-GEN}\xspace, we consider two cases.\\ i) ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}=\emptyset$: When \text{ID-GEN}\xspace visits step 7 for the first time, we have ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}=\emptyset$. In that case, we first update our dataset $\mathcal{D}[\mathbf{V}]\sim P(\mathbf{v})$ to samples from $\mathcal{D}'\sim P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}( \mathbf{v})$, and then we recurse on the query $P'_{\mathbf{x}\cap S'}(\mathbf{y})$ over the graph $G_{S'}$. Also, $\mathbf{X}_Z$ is outside the c-component $S'$. Therefore we generate a dataset from $\mathcal{D}'\sim P_{\mathbf{x}_Z}(S')$ via running directly the $\texttt{ConditionalGMs(.)}\xspace$ of the \text{ID-GEN}\xspace algorithm, Algorithm~\ref{alg:step1}: $\texttt{ConditionalGMs}(S', X_Z, G, \mathcal{D}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, {\hat{{G}}})$. This is attainable via the inductive assumption and Lemma \ref{lem:termination}. The only divergence from ID during the generation of $\mathcal{D}'$ is that ID presumes pre-specified fixed values for $\mathbf{X}_Z$, where we train a sampling mechanism that is agnostic a priori to the specific choice of $\mathbf{X}_Z$. To sidestep this issue, we generate a dataset with all possible values of $\mathbf{X}_Z$ and be sure to record the values of $\mathbf{X}_Z$ in the dataset $\mathcal{D}'[\mathbf{X}_Z, S']$.
nodes.statement_short: First visit: generate $D'\sim P_{x_Z}(S')$ with ConditionalGMs over all values of $X_Z$.

nodes.name: Case: X-hat non-empty
nodes.statement: ii) ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \neq \emptyset$: When \text{ID-GEN}\xspace has visited step 7 already once and thus ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}\neq \emptyset$. We consider ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ along with $\mathbf{X}_Z$ when generating $\mathcal{D}'$ this time. More precisely, we update our dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, \mathbf{V}]\sim P({\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$ to samples from $\mathcal{D}'\sim P_{\mathbf{x}_Z \cup {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}}(\mathbf{x}_z, {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}, \mathbf{v})$. Rest of the steps follow similarly as the above case. We record the new $\mathbf{X}_Z$ in ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ and carry them in $\mathcal{D}'[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S']$ and ${\hat{{G}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Later visits: generate data from $P_{x_Z\cup\hat x}$ and record $X_Z$ in $\hat X$.

nodes.name: Map ID's recursive call
nodes.statement: Next, we need to map the recursive call $ID(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap S', P', G)$ to \text{ID-GEN}\xspace. \text{ID-GEN}\xspace sends the same parameters $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}\cap S'$ and $G$ as ID. Now, equivalent to passing the distribution $P'$ of ID, we pass the dataset $\mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S']$ sampled from this distribution, including the intervened values for ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ used to obtain this dataset. According to Lemma~\ref{lem:same-dist-graph}, this dataset is sampled from $P'$ if we fix to a specific value ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$. Finally, ID algorithm uses specific value of $\mathbf{X}_Z$ and then ignores those variables from $\mathbf{X}$ and $G$ for rest of the recursion. On the other hand, \text{ID-GEN}\xspace saves $\mathbf{X}_Z$ in ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ as ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}= {\hat{\mathbf{X}}} \cup \mathbf{X}_Z$ and keeps ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ connected to ${\hat{{G}}}$ with incoming edges cut, i.e., $G_{S',\overline{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}}$ for the next recursive calls since \text{ID-GEN}\xspace utilizes ${\hat{\mathbf{X}}}$ and the topological order in ${\hat{{G}}}$ at the base cases (step 1 and 6).
nodes.statement_short: Pass the same $Y, X\cap S', G$ with the generated dataset, which follows $P'$ by Lemma D.15.

nodes.name: Recurse
nodes.statement: By the inductive assumption, we can generate a correct sampling network from the call $\text{ID-GEN}\xspace(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X} \setminus \mathbf{X}_Z , G_{S'}, \mathcal{D}[{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}, S], {{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}, {\hat{{G}}}_{\{S', \overline{{\hat{\mathbf{X}}}}\}} $), and hence the returned sampling graph is correct for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}).$
nodes.statement_short: The recursive network is correct by the inductive assumption.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since we have shown that every recursion of \text{ID-GEN}\xspace ultimately terminates in a base case, that all the base cases provide correct sampling graphs, and that correct sampling graphs can be constructed in each step assuming the recursive calls are correct, we conclude that \text{ID-GEN}\xspace returns the correct sampling graph for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}).$
nodes.statement_short: Termination, correct base cases and correct recursive steps give a correct network.

nodes.name: ID-GEN Completeness
nodes.statement: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is complete.
conclusions: \text{ID-GEN}\xspace is complete.
nodes.label: th:id-dag-complete

nodes.name: Proof of ID-GEN completeness
nodes.statement: Suppose we are given a causal query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ as input to sample from. We prove that if \text{ID-GEN}\xspace fails, then the query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is non identifiable, implying that it is not possible to train conditional models on observational data and correctly sample from the interventional distribution $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$. If \text{ID-GEN}\xspace reaches step 5, it returns \texttt{FAIL}. According to the lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, ID reaches at step 5 if and only if \text{ID-GEN}\xspace reaches at step 5. Step 5 is also the \texttt{FAIL} case of the ID algorithm. Since ID is complete and returns \texttt{FAIL} at Step 5, the query $P_{x}(y)$ is not identifiable.
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive via ID: ID-GEN fails only at step 5, where ID fails, and ID is complete.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Suppose we are given a causal query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ as input to sample from. We prove that if \text{ID-GEN}\xspace fails, then the query $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ is non identifiable, implying that it is not possible to train conditional models on observational data and correctly sample from the interventional distribution $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Show that a failure of ID-GEN implies non-identifiability.

nodes.name: Failure at step 5
nodes.statement: If \text{ID-GEN}\xspace reaches step 5, it returns \texttt{FAIL}. According to the lemma~\ref{lem:mirror}, ID reaches at step 5 if and only if \text{ID-GEN}\xspace reaches at step 5.
nodes.statement_short: ID-GEN fails only at step 5, which ID reaches too (Lemma D.11).

nodes.name: Conclude via ID's completeness
nodes.statement: Step 5 is also the \texttt{FAIL} case of the ID algorithm. Since ID is complete and returns \texttt{FAIL} at Step 5, the query $P_{x}(y)$ is not identifiable.
nodes.statement_short: ID is complete and fails there, so the query is not identifiable.

nodes.name: Maximal rule-2 set (Shpitser & Pearl)
nodes.statement: For any $G$ and any conditional effect $P_{{X}}({Y}|{W})$ there exists a unique maximal set ${Z}= \{Z \in {W}|P_{{X}}({Y}|{W}) = P_{{X,Z}}({Y|W} \setminus {Z})\}$ such that rule 2 applies to ${Z}$ in $G$ for $P_{{X}}({Y}|{W})$. In other words, $P_{{X}}({Y}|{W}) = P_{{X,Z}}({Y|W \setminus Z)}$.
assumptions: any $G$ and any conditional effect $P_{{X}}({Y}|{W})$
conclusions: there exists a unique maximal set ${Z}= \{Z \in {W}|P_{{X}}({Y}|{W}) = P_{{X,Z}}({Y|W} \setminus {Z})\}$ such that rule 2 applies to ${Z}$ in $G$ for $P_{{X}}({Y}|{W})$
nodes.label: theorem20

nodes.name: Identifiability of conditional effects (Shpitser & Pearl)
nodes.statement: Let $P_{{X}}({Y}|{W})$ be such that every $W \in {W} $ has a back-door path to $Y$ in $G\setminus {X}$ given ${W}\setminus \{W\}$. Then $P_{{X}}({Y|W})$ is identifiable in $G$ if and only if $P_{{X}}({Y, W})$ is identifiable in $G$.
assumptions: $P_{{X}}({Y}|{W})$ be such that every $W \in  {W} $ has a back-door path to $Y$ in $G\setminus {X}$ given ${W}\setminus \{W\}$
conclusions: $P_{{X}}({Y|W})$ is identifiable in $G$ if and only if $P_{{X}}({Y, W})$ is identifiable in $G$
nodes.label: theorem21

nodes.name: Napkin-MNIST attribute sets
nodes.statement: First lets define the sets \begin{itemize} \item $\texttt{COLORS}:= \{\texttt{red, green, blue, yellow, magenta, cyan}\}$. \item $\texttt{RG\_COLORS}:= \{\texttt{red, green}\}$. \item $\texttt{THICKNESSES}:= \{\texttt{thin, regular, thick}\}$. \item $\texttt{DIGITS}:= \{0,\dots, 9\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case

nodes.name: Napkin-MNIST variables and supports
nodes.statement: And then the definitions and support of each of the variables in our distribution: \begin{itemize} \item (Latent) $\texttt{Color} \in \texttt{COLORS}$. \item (Latent) $\texttt{Thickness} \in \texttt{THICKNESSES}$. \item $W_1 \in \texttt{DIGITS}\times \texttt{COLORS}\times \texttt{THICKNESSES}$ \item $W_2 \in \texttt{DIGITS}\times \texttt{RG\_COLORS}$. \item $X \in \texttt{DIGITS}\times \texttt{COLORS}\times \texttt{THICKNESSES}$ \item $Y \in \texttt{DIGITS}\times \texttt{COLORS}\times \texttt{THICKNESSES}$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case
nodes.statement_short: Latent Color and Thickness, and observed $W_1, X, Y$ (digit, color, thickness) and $W_2$ (digit, restricted color).

nodes.name: Noise probability p
nodes.statement: A key hyperparameter is a noise-probability $p$. This defines the probability that any variable flips to a uniform probability.
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case

nodes.name: Noising function eta_p, restriction map R and uniform choice U
nodes.statement: To ease notation, we define the function $\eta_p(v, S)$ defined as \[ \eta_p(v, S) := \begin{cases} v & \text{with probability } 1-p\\ U(S) & \text{otherwise } \end{cases} \] and we define the mapping $R: \texttt{COLORS}\to \texttt{RESTRICTED\_COLORS}$ as \[ R(c) := \begin{cases} \texttt{red} & \text{if } c\in \{\texttt{red, green, blue}\}\\ \texttt{green} & \text{otherwise } \end{cases} \] Where $U(S)$ means a uniformly random choice of $S$.
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case
nodes.statement_short: $\eta_p(v,S)$ keeps $v$ with probability $1-p$ and otherwise draws uniformly from $S$; $R$ maps colors to red/green.

nodes.name: Napkin-MNIST data generation procedure (discrete)
nodes.statement: Then our data generation procedure follows the following steps: \begin{itemize} \item $\texttt{Color} := U(\texttt{COLORS})$ \item $\texttt{Thickness}:= U(\texttt{THICKNESSES})$ \item $W_1 := \big(U(\texttt{DIGITS}),\quad \eta_p(\texttt{Color}, \texttt{COLORS}),\quad \eta_p(\texttt{Thickness}, \texttt{THICKNESSES})\big)$ \item $W_2 := \big(\eta_p(W_{1}._{digit}, \texttt{DIGITS}),\quad \eta_p(R(W_{1}._{color}, \texttt{RG\_COLORS})\big)$ \item $X := \big(\eta_p(W_{2}._{digit}, \texttt{DIGITS}),\quad \eta_p(W_{2}._{color}, \texttt{RG\_COLORS}),\quad \eta_p(\texttt{Thickness}, \texttt{THICKNESSES})\big)$ \item $Y := \big(\eta_p(X._{digit}, \texttt{DIGITS}),\quad \eta_p(\texttt{Color}, \texttt{COLORS}),\quad \eta_p(X._{thickness}, \texttt{THICKNESSES})\big)$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case
nodes.statement_short: Sample latent color and thickness, then generate $W_1, W_2, X, Y$ in order, each attribute copied from its parent through the noising function $\eta_p$.

nodes.name: Generated SCM is the Napkin graph
nodes.statement: It is easy to verify that this describes the Napkin graph, as each only $\texttt{Color, Thickness}$ are latent and each variable only depends on its parents in the SCM.
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case
conclusions: this describes the Napkin graph

nodes.statement: Secondly, observe that this structural causal model is separable with respect to digits, colors, and thicknesses.
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case
conclusions: this structural causal model is separable with respect to digits, colors, and thicknesses

nodes.name: Why the SCM is separable
nodes.statement: Since each digit only depends on parent \emph{digits}, each color only depends on parent \emph{colors}, and each thickness depends only on parent \emph{thicknesses}, these can all be considered separately.
nodes.section: F.2.1 Data generation procedure: discrete case

nodes.name: Analytic attribute-agreement probabilities
nodes.statement: For example, assuming we have hyperparameter of random noise equal to $p$, we can compute the following quantities analytically on the discrete dataset as: \begin{itemize} \item $P[X_{d} = {W_2}_{d}] = 1-p + \frac{p}{10}$ \item $P[X._{c} = {W_2}_{c}] = 1-p + \frac{p}{10}$ \item $P[X_{t}={W_1}_{t}] = (1-p + \frac{p}{3})^2 + \big(\frac{p}{3}\big)^2 * 2$ \item $P[Y_{d} = X_{d}] = 1-p + \frac{p}{10}$ \item $P[Y_{c} = {W_1}_{c}] = (1-p + \frac{p}{6})^2 + big(\frac{p}{6}\big)^2 * 5$ \item $P[Y_{t}=X_{t}] = 1-p + \frac{p}{3}$ \end{itemize} where $V_d, V_c, V_t$ refer to the digit, color, and thickness attributes respectively.
assumptions: we have hyperparameter of random noise equal to $p$
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form probabilities that a child's digit, color or thickness matches its parent's under noise $p$.

nodes.name: Noising agreement formulas
nodes.statement: In a discrete distribution with support $S$ and $|S|=K$: \begin{itemize} \item $P[\eta_p(z, S) = z] = 1-p + \frac{p}{K}$ \item $P[\eta_p(z, S) = \eta_p(z, S)] = (1-p+\frac{p}{K})^2 + \Big(\frac{p}{K}\Big)^2 * (K-1)$ \end{itemize} where in the second equation, it is assumed that $\eta_p(\cdot, \cdot)$ are two independent noising procedures.

nodes.name: IDC-GEN
nodes.statement: \footnotesize \caption{\footnotesize \text{IDC-GEN}\xspace($\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z}, \mathcal{D}, G$) } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE \textbf{Input:} target ${Y}$, intervention ${X}$ , conditioning set ${Z}$. training data $\mathcal{D}$, $G$. \STATE {\bfseries Output:} A DAG of trained model to sample from $P_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{Y|Z})$. \IF{ $\exists \alpha \in Z$ such that $({Y} \perp \!\!\! \perp \alpha| {X}, {Z}\setminus \{\alpha\})_{G_{\overline{{X}}, \underline{\alpha}}}$} \STATE \textbf{return} \text{IDC-GEN}\xspace(${Y}, {X} \cup \{\alpha\}, {Z}\setminus \{\alpha\}, \mathcal{D}, G$) \ELSE \STATE $H_1$= \text{ID-GEN}\xspace(${Y\cup Z}, {X}, \mathcal{D}, {\hat{\mathbf{X}}}=\emptyset, {\hat{{G}}}=G$) \STATE $\mathcal{D}' \sim H_1({X})$ \STATE $H_2 = \emptyset$ \STATE Add node $(X, \emptyset)$ and $(Z, \emptyset)$ to $H_2$ \STATE Let $M_{Y}$ be a model trained on $\{Y, X, Z\}\sim \mathcal{D}'$ such that $M_{Y}(X,Z)\sim P'(Y|X,Z)$ i.e., $ M_{Y}(X,Z)\sim P_{X}(Y|Z)$ \STATE Add node $(Y, M_Y)$ to $H_2$ \STATE Add edge $X\rightarrow Y$ and $Z\rightarrow Y$ to $H_2$ \STATE \textbf{return} $H_2$ \ENDIF \end{algorithmic}
output: A DAG of trained model to sample from $P_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{Y|Z})$.
nodes.statement_short: Move conditioning variables into the intervention by rule 2, sample the joint with ID-GEN, then train one conditional model for $Y$ given $X, Z$.

nodes.name: ID algorithm
nodes.statement: \footnotesize \caption{\footnotesize ID($\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}, P, G$) } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE \textbf{Input:} $\mathbf{y}$, $\mathbf{x}$ value assignments , distribution $P$, $G$. \STATE {\bfseries Output:} Expression for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ in terms of $P$ or Fail$(F, F')$. \IF[\textcolor{blue}{Step:1}]{$\mathbf{x}=\emptyset$ } \STATE \textbf{Return } $\sum_{\mathbf{v}\setminus \mathbf{y}}P(\mathbf{v})$ \ENDIF \IF[\textcolor{blue}{Step:2}]{$\mathbf{V}\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_{G} \neq \emptyset$} \STATE \textbf{Return} \textbf{ID}($\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}\cap An(\mathbf{Y})_G, \sum_{\mathbf{V}\setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_G}P, G_{An(\mathbf{Y})}$) \ENDIF \STATE Let $\mathbf{W} = (\mathbf{V} \setminus \mathbf{X}) \setminus An(\mathbf{Y})_{G_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}$ \COMMENT{\textcolor{blue}{Step:3}} \IF{$\mathbf{W} \ne \emptyset$} \STATE \textbf{Return ID}$(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}\cup \mathbf{w}, P, G)$ \ENDIF \IF[\textcolor{blue}{Step:4}]{$C(G \setminus \mathbf{X}) = \{S_1, \ldots, S_{k}\}$} \STATE \textbf{Return} $\sum_{\mathbf{v\setminus (y \cup x)} } \prod_i ID(s_i, \mathbf{v}\setminus s_i, P, G)$ \ENDIF \IF{$C(G \setminus \mathbf{X}) = \{S\}$} \IF[\textcolor{blue}{Step:5}]{$C(G) = \{G\}$} \STATE \textbf{Return FAIL}$(G, G \cap S)$ \ENDIF \IF[\textcolor{blue}{Step:6}]{$S \in C(G)$} \STATE \textbf{Return} $\sum_{s\setminus \mathbf{y}}\prod_{\{i | V_{i} \in S\}} P(v_{i} | v_{\pi}^{i-1})$ \ENDIF \IF[\textcolor{blue}{Step:7}]{$\exists S' $ s.t. $S\subset S'\in C(G)$} \STATE \textbf{Return ID}$(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}\cap S', {P}= \prod_{\{i | V_{i} \in S'\}}P(V_{i}| V_{\pi}^{(i-1)}\cap S', v_{\pi}^{(i-1)}\setminus S' ), G_{S'})$ \ENDIF \ENDIF \end{algorithmic}
output: Expression for $P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})$ in terms of $P$ or Fail$(F, F')$.
nodes.statement_short: Recursive sound and complete identification of $P_x(y)$ from $P$ via seven graphical steps (marginalize, add interventions, c-component factorization, fail, base cases).

nodes.name: IDC algorithm
nodes.statement: \footnotesize \caption{\footnotesize IDC(${Y}, {X}, {Z}, P, G$) } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE \textbf{Input:} $x,y,z$ value assignments, $P$ a probability distribution, $G$ a causal diagram (an I-map of $P$). \STATE {\bfseries Output:} Expression for $P_{{X}}({Y|Z})$ in terms of $P$ or Fail(F, F'). \IF{ $\exists \alpha \in Z$ such that $({Y} \perp \!\!\! \perp \alpha| {X}, {Z}\setminus \{\alpha\})_{G_{\overline{{X}}, \underline{\alpha}}}$} \STATE \textbf{return} IDC(${Y}, {X} \cup \{\alpha\}, {Z}\setminus \{\alpha\}, \mathcal{D}, G$) \ELSE \STATE let $P'$ = ID($\mathbf{y \cup z,x}, P, G$) \STATE return $P'/ \sum_{\mathbf{y}} P'$ \ENDIF \end{algorithmic}

output: Expression for $P_{{X}}({Y|Z})$ in terms of $P$ or Fail(F, F').
